text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English novelist EMILY BRONTE, who wrote "Wuthering Heights", was born in 1818. It was her only book and was published in 1847, the year before she died.

The man who became known as the "criminal of the century", FREDERICK DEEMING, was born in England in 1853. He was a fraud, a bigamist and a murderer. DEEMING commuted between Australia and England. He murdered two of his wives and four children, and was even accused of being "Jack the Ripper".
American car manufacturer, HENRY FORD, was born in 1863.
Professor CYRIL NORTHCOTE PARKINSON, who devised "Parkinson's Law", was born in 1909. His law says that work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
Australian poet, JOHN BLIGHT, whose works include "My Beachcombing Days", was born in 1913.

Canadian singer/songwriter, PAUL ANKA, was born in 1941. He began his show business career in the 1950s while he was still at school. In 1956 he started work on the song "Diana". The inspiration for the song was the Anka family's babysitter DIANA AYOUB, who was 18. Paul was just 15. The song became his first million dollar hit in 1957. His many other hits include "I Love You Baby" (1957), "Lonely Boy" (1959), "Puppy Love" (1960) and "You're Having My Baby" (1974). He was prolific songwriter for other singers. He wrote the English lyrics for the French song "My Way" which became a world hit for FRANK SINATRA.
British bass player with Jethro Tull, JEFFREY HAMMOND-HAMMOND, was born in 1946.

Austrian born actor, ARNOLD SCWARZENEGGER, was born in 1947. The former "Mr Universe" has had a string of block-buster movies including the "Predator" and "Terminator" series, which followed his appearances as "Conan The Barbarian".
United States singer, JOYCE JONES, was born in 1949. She sang with 'First Choice' and their hits included "Armed and Extremely Dangerous" (1973) and "Smarty Pants" (1973).

British singer/songwriter, KATE BUSH, was born in 1958. After being groomed by DAVE GILMOUR of 'Pink Floyd', KATE BUSH had her first hit in 1978 with "Wuthering Heights". Further hits included "The Man With The Child In His Eyes" (1978), and "Babooshka" (1980).
British athlete, DALEY THOMPSON, who won Olympic gold twice for the decathlon, was born in 1958.
** EVENTS **
1718 : WILLIAM PENN, English Quaker leader who founded
the American state of Pennsylvania, died.
1858 : British explorer, JOHN HANNING SPEKE, named the
great lake he discovered in the heart of Africa after Queen VICTORIA.
1898 : OTTO von BISMARCK, founder and first chancellor of
the German Empire, died.
1924 : Australia had its most successful Olympics to
date. The medal tally from the Paris Games was three gold, one silver and two bronze. Gold medallists included teenage swimmer, ANDREW 'BOY' CHARLTON in the 1500 metres freestyle. The 17
year-old from Sydney picked up two other medals. A bronze in the 400 metres and a silver in the 4 X 200 metres relay.
1930 : The first ever soccer World Cup was won by
Uruguay, beating Argentina 4-2.
1935 : The first Penguin book was published, starting the
paperback revolution. The idea came from Sir ALLEN LANE, who wanted to provide "a whole book for the price of 10 cigarettes". The first one to be issued was "Ariel" by ANDRE MAUROIS.
1945 : The U.S. cruiser Indianapolis was sunk by a
Japanese submarine killing over 800. It was returning to the U.S. after delivering nuclear material for the atomic bomb.
1947 : The Kon Tiki raft's trip across the South Pacific

came to end on the Polynesian island of Puka Puka, just east of Tahiti. THOR HEYERDAHL set out from Peru to support his theory that the first settlers in Polynesia were of South American origin. The raft was made of balsa wood lashed together, and was crewed by HEYERDAHL and five companions.
1949 : British warship HMS Amethyst made its escape down
the Yangtze River, having been refused a safe passage by Chinese Communists after a three-month standoff.
1951 : Crisis talks were held in Sydney over Australia's

inflation rate. Those involved included MENZIES, FADDEN, the State Premiers and the ACTU. In the following months the basic wage was increased by two shillings to combat the rising prices, and in a horror budget the government greatly increased sales tax.
1959 : Part-Aborigine, RUPERT MAX STUART, was given a
reprieve from hanging for the murder of a nine-year-old girl. A Royal Commission into the case commuted the original death sentence to life imprisonment, but the inquiry supported the guilty verdict.
1959 : Fashion designer, YVES ST LAURENT, apparently
overcame his dislike of knees to raise the hemlines on his new season's creations. The collection included puffed skirts and high, built-up hair styles.
1963 : British double-agent KIM PHILBY surfaced in
Moscow, seven months after his disappearance in Beirut.
1966 : England beat Germany 4-2 at Wembley to win the
football World Cup.
1967 : A new four digit post code was introduced in
Australia to help with mail sorting.
1973 : The 11-year battle for the victims of the drug
thalidomide ended with compensation payments of 20 million pounds sterling.
1979 : In Cambodia, Khmer Rouge chief POL POT was accused
of murdering three million Cambodians.
1980 : The Republic of Vanuatu (formerly the
Franco-British condominium of New Hebrides) achieved its independence.
1987 : Saudi Arabian police opened fire on Iranian
zealots during the annual pilgrimage to Mecca.
1990 : British conservative politician IAN GOW, who was
on the IRA's hitlist, was killed by a car bomb. The 53-year-old politician was one of the most outspoken critics of IRA terrorism.
1991 : Rain failed to stop the open-air concert by

LUCIANO PAVAROTTI in London's Hyde Park. The free concert, to mark PAVAROTTI's 30th anniversary in opera, attracted more than 150,000 people, including Princess DIANA. The concert was televised live to an estimated 400 million people in 33 countries.
1993 : In Geneva peace talks, Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and
Croats agreed to create a new "union" of three ethnic republics.
1994 : Zaire declared its eastern region, swamped by 1.7
million Rwandan refugees, a disaster region.
1996 : CLAUDETTE COLBERT, queen of 1930s Hollywood
comedies, died. COLBERT won an Academy Award for best actress for her performance in the screwball comedy, "It Happened One Night", in 1934. She was 92.
